entities.name: Asad ibn Hashim
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Asad ibn Hashim (d. c. 600 CE) was a revered patriarch of the Banu Hashim clan, a prominent sub-clan of the Quraysh tribe, which dominated the city of Mecca in the late 6th century CE. His primary historical significance stems not from military conquests or vast commercial empires, but from his pivotal familial connections to the nascent Islamic faith. He was the maternal uncle of the Prophet Muhammad, as his sister Fatima bint Amr was Muhammad's grandmother. More critically, Asad was the father of Fatima bint Asad, who became the wife of Abu Talib and the mother of Ali ibn Abi Talib, one of Islam's most revered figures and the fourth Rashidun Caliph. His status as a leading figure within the powerful Quraysh tribe provided a crucial social and political backdrop for the emergence of Islam.

Born into a lineage deeply intertwined with the custodianship of the Kaaba, Asad ibn Hashim held considerable social standing and influence within Meccan society, which was then a thriving commercial and religious hub of the Arabian Peninsula. While specific details of his life are sparse in pre-Islamic records, his role as a prominent merchant and elder of the Banu Hashim is well-documented in early Islamic tradition. He was known for his generosity and hospitality, traits highly valued in Bedouin culture, and his household was a center of tribal life. His daughter, Fatima bint Asad, was instrumental in raising the young Muhammad after the death of his mother and grandfather, offering him shelter and maternal care.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Asad ibn Hashim holds significant regional and thematic importance due to his direct ancestral links to the Prophet Muhammad and Ali ibn Abi Talib, figures central to the founding and early development of Islam. His role as a respected patriarch of the Banu Hashim clan provided crucial social context for the rise of a new world religion.
